pass_a_gloss: …some opposing copies; for it is set down neither among the Seventy nor among others. Under chapter sixteen: Wrath of a king is a messenger of death; yet a wise man will win him over — that is, if the holy person is without passion; otherwise the wrath has to be taken allegorically. Under chapter twenty-five: But in places of ungodly people, humans are seized. And their places are also the meetings of the heretics. Under chapter thirty: Three things are impossible for me to grasp. Impossible, for someone being brought into scientific understanding, is a theorem; and impossible for a human being is to contemplate the things above the human and to grasp them, for instance the healing of the crab, even if angels know that healing; and impossible for someone to grasp is also what in no way exists and is not able to come into being, for instance that three should be four. It seems, then, to have been spoken about things that do not exist. For when an eagle has not left tracks while flying about the air — tracks analogous to those left in sandy ground by those who step on it — it is impossible for that to be grasped; so also in the case of a snake: on easily marked earth it is possible for paths to be grasped, but not on the rock. And paths of a ship that travels the deep. Perhaps in these lines the ship ought to be named Jesus and his disciples, and sometimes them alone; not traveling the deep — for at once the boat came to be upon the land toward which they were going, by divine power. But a ship that does not bear Jesus
pass_b_english: …in certain manuscript copies; for it stands neither in the Seventy nor in the others.
Chapter 16: “A king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will propitiate him”—if the holy one is free of passion; or else the wrath must be read allegorically.
Chapter 25: “But in the places of the ungodly people are caught.” Their places are also the gatherings of the heretics.

Chapter 30: “Three things are impossible for me to understand.” For someone being led into scientific grasp, a theorem can be impossible; for a human it is impossible to contemplate and know what is beyond the human—say, the healing of the crab, even if angels know it; and it is impossible for anyone to understand what in no way exists and cannot come to be, for example that three is four. So the saying seems to concern things that do not exist. When an eagle leaves no tracks while flying through the air—unlike the tracks left in sandy ground by those who step on it—those tracks cannot be grasped; so also with a snake: on yielding earth paths can be known, but not on rock. “And the paths of a ship going through the sea.” Perhaps here the ship should be called Jesus and his disciples, and sometimes them alone—not sea-going, for at once the boat was at the land toward which they were going, by divine power. But a ship that does not carry Jesus
